There's tons of pros and cons to defined benefit vs defined contribution. I personally think its not all that close. I would (and do) prefer defined contribution if i were given the option.

1. as max and you already said. job mobility and portability of these plans doesn't work as its set up. Its simply not in line with the current way the job market works. 

2. Its fairly common for pensions to not include CLOA's for inflation etc. A fixed pension giving you $50k per year in 2000 is at least half as valuable as it was then.

3.  there's funding sponsor risk. There are back stops from ERISA and other things but if the company goes bankrupt that's a real potential problem and would likely lead to less money for many people in that pension plan. For public pensions its not as worrisome because they'll just increase taxes on citizens to fund it (or cut benefits from the pensioners to better balance the books)

4. Way way wayyy less flexibility. Cant change withdrawal rate. Cant change your investments to dial up or down the risk. You basically get a fixed annuity (which isn't neccessarily bad)

5. If you want that fixed annuity you can use your retirement funds in defined contribution world to buy exactly that! 

If you are going to spend the bulk of your adult life working for a stable and successful employer that will never go out of business and offers you a pension with CLOAs... that is an *excellent* retirement solution. Basically 10 out of 10. but that's a lot of "ifs" and it doesn't automatically make them the best retirement saving system for everyone or even a flexible workforce where the average person changes their job every ~5 years.

Not to mention the fact that most pensions are underfunded in the US -- much like social security.

Interest burden = rate × debt. US public debt is ~100% of GDP and interest is now over 3% of GDP, a record, so the rate the system can tolerate falls.

Treasury has also let bills climb to ~23% of marketable debt (TBAC's comfort zone is 15-20%) by funding deficits short instead of terming out the debt. So, more of the US government's interest bill now floats with the Fed, a classic on-ramp to fiscal dominance.

The GFC set the modern standard for bailouts (2008, 2020, 2023). GS's Financial Conditions Index (yields, credit spreads, equities, dollar; higher = tighter; chart below) has never again been allowed to tighten as badly as 2009. With little political appetite for real belt-tightening, the path of least resistance is monetization.

That's why we're constructive on scarce assets like Gold and Bitcoin over multi-year periods.

(Although BTC's flat 5-year record is a fair rebuttal at this point.)

Treasury has also let bills climb to ~23% of marketable debt (TBAC's comfort zone is 15-20%) by funding deficits short instead of terming out the debt. So, more of the US government's interest bill now floats with the Fed, a classic on-ramp to fiscal dominance.

The GFC set the modern standard for bailouts (2008, 2020, 2023). GS's Financial Conditions Index (yields, credit spreads, equities, dollar; higher = tighter; chart below) has never again been allowed to tighten as badly as 2009. With little political appetite for real belt-tightening, the path of least resistance is monetization.

That's why we're constructive on scarce assets like Gold and Bitcoin over multi-year periods.

(Although BTC's flat 5-year record is a fair rebuttal at this point.)

I would argue that the first chart below is probably the single most investment-relevant chart for Chinese markets right now.

Strong exports have been the key factor keeping Chinese growth resilient this year, thereby reducing the urgency for policymakers to stimulate domestic demand.

But as the chart shows, roughly 40% of that export strength has been driven by the global AI build-out, particularly in the US. Any slowdown in AI capex would therefore disproportionately hurt Chinese exports at a time when domestic demand is already in recession.

In other words, bad news for AI could actually be good news for the Chinese stimulus trade: it would increase the likelihood of a stronger policy response from Beijing to shore up domestic demand, particularly consumption.

For global investors looking to hedge against a potential AI selloff, I believe Chinese consumer stocks are becoming increasingly attractive, especially following this year’s selloff.
